clinician.trajectory_summary: A 49-year-old woman presented with 20 days of difficulty finding words and unresponsiveness, found to have a chronic cortical infarct on MRI. Initial workup ruled out large vessel stenosis and general laboratory studies were normal. A transesophageal echocardiogram later revealed a patent foramen ovale (PFO). Immunological examination, performed significantly later, showed positive antibodies to vimentin/CL complex and anti-annexin A5 antibody (non-criteria antiphospholipid antibodies). Criteria antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin IgG/IgM, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I IgG/IgM) were largely negative, with only anti-beta2-glycoprotein I IgA being positive, supporting the 'seronegative' classification. This constellation of findings led to the diagnosis of Seronegative Antiphospholipid Syndrome. The patient was subsequently treated with long-term low-dose aspirin and warfarin, and her stroke symptoms have not recurred.
